d: The sound of casual playing on a musical instrument
ety: From toot + -le, frequentative.
s: The glamour of the sawdust world, the cheers of the crowd, the smell of hot dogs and cotton candy, the blare and tootle of the midway—he envied the gypsy family, here today and gone tomorrow.

d: A studio especially for an artist or designer
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French atelier, from Middle French astelier, from astelle (“small piece of wood, etc., to hold a broken bone in place, splint”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱs- (“axis; axle”) via Latin assula) + -ier (suffix denoting the location of an abode). Compare typologically Latin harēna, whence arena.
s: At the meeting of the Society, February 6, it was stated that red glass was preferable to yellow for the windows of photographic ateliers.

d: Giving careful attention to detail; hard to please; excessively concerned with cleanliness
ety: Borrowed from Latin fastīdiōsus (“passive: that feels disgust, disdainful, scornful, fastidious; active: that causes disgust, disgusting, loathsome”), from fastīdium (“a loathing, aversion, disgust, niceness of taste, daintiness, etc.”), perhaps for *fastutidium, from fastus (“disdain, haughtiness, arrogance, disgust”) + taedium (“disgust”). Cf. French fastidieux.
s: As she cleaned the room daily, she knew it was against his fastidious nature to bring or have food in his room.

d: An etching made by a process that makes it resemble a water color
ety: Borrowed from Italian acquatinta (literally “dyed water”).
s: Aquatint is a laborious process that involves acids and resistants and emphasizes tone over line.

d: Effusively or insincerely emotional
ety: From schmaltz + -y.
s: “In France, it has the reputation of being a typically American mixture of clichés and of schmaltz,” he wrote in an email. “Clichés about us don’t interest us, and the French are not very schmaltzy.”

d: A demon that enters the body of a living person and controls that body’s behavior
ety: From Yiddish דיבוק (dibek), from Hebrew דבק (dovek, “cling”).
s: And who am I? A dybbuk—a demon of all shapes and no shape. My profession is forced entry into the minds of mortals; my speciality is Jews.

d: A strip of pleated material used as a decoration or a trim
ety: Probably of North Germanic origin, from Norwegian flunsa (“hurry”), perhaps ultimately imitative. Or, perhaps formed on the pattern of pounce, bounce.
s: Then he looked from her to some gayer figures moving along the road with flutters of bright streamers and flounces

d: A person who is of equal standing with another in a group
ety: From Middle English comper, from Middle French comper, from Latin compater, compatrem. Doublet of compere as well as compadre and goombah. Influenced by folk-etymological analysis as com- + peer.
s: And him thus answer'd soon his bold compeer.

d: A style that involves indirect ways of expressing things
ety: From Ancient Greek περίφρασις (períphrasis).
s: Native speakers use periphrases like "did not go" where a language learner might use "went not".

d: A short movement coming between the major sections of a symphony
ety: Borrowed from Italian intermezzo. Doublet of intermede and intermedium
s: Thespis’ single actor served only to create an intermezzo between choral chants.

d: Composed of animal fat
ety: From international scientific vocabulary, from New Latin adipōsus, from Latin adeps (“fat, lard”). By surface analysis, adip- + -ose; Latin adeps (“fat, lard”) is probably related to Umbrian 𐌀𐌛𐌄𐌐𐌄𐌔 (ařepes, “offerings of fat”) since 𐌛 (ř) in Umbrian regularly represents an earlier *d.
s: They will attack the problem specifically at key sites in the brain, digestive system, and adipose organs.

d: A loose-fitting white ecclesiastical vestment with wide sleeves
ety: Inherited from Middle English surplys, from Old French surpeliz, from Medieval Latin superpelliceum, from Latin super (“over”) and pellis (“fur”).
s: He was a wide man and looked wider in his surplice, especially from our pew, which was close up under the pulpit.

d: A whistling sound when breathing (usually heard on inspiration); indicates obstruction of the trachea or larynx
ety: From Latin strīdor (“shrill or harsh sound”), from strīdō (“make a shrill or harsh sound”).
s: Her breath-holding increased in duration to almost a minute; her expirations became complicated by stridor, forced retching, and forced phonations ('Oouuggh!').

d: Marked by rude or peremptory shortness
ety: The adjective is borrowed from French brusque, from Italian brusco (“abrupt, sudden, brusque; brisk; eager; sour, tart; unripe; grim-looking”); further etymology unknown. The verb is derived from the adjective.
s: They admired in each other a brusque self-assurance and artless candor that others often perceived as arrogant.

d: One who professes great sensitivity to the beauty of art and nature
ety: From Ancient Greek αἰσθητής (aisthētḗs, “one who perceives”).
s: Because what the aesthete does is to say, “oh, I can transform any unpleasant experience into a moment of beauty.”

d: Difficult to handle or use especially because of size or weight
ety: From Late Middle English combrous (“causing obstruction; clumsy; obstructed; bothersome, difficult; burdensome, onerous; serious; causing trouble, troublesome; dangerous; immoral; unjust, wrongful; upset”) [and other forms], from komber, kumbre (“distress; destruction”) + -ous (suffix forming adjectives). The English word is analysable as cumber + -ous.
s: This class of apparatus, often called today the "poste classique", gave first-class service in every respect but became cumbrous if a large layout had to be controlled.

d: Delicate and intricate ornamentation (usually in gold or silver or other fine twisted wire)
ety: From French filigrane, from Italian filigrana, from Latin fīlum (“thread”) + grānum (“grain”).
s: To carry pure death in an earring, a casket, / A signet, a fan-mount, a filigree basket!

d: Like twilight; dim
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin crepusculum + -ar.
s: That's why cats are crepuscular — most active at dawn and dusk — because mice and rats forage for food during these hours when fewer of their natural enemies are around.

d: A meddler who offers unwanted advice to others
ety: From kibitz + -er.
s: Did I ask you what you thought about my cards, you kibitzer?

d: A sandal with flat heels and an upper of woven leather straps
ety: Borrowed from Mexican Spanish huarache, guarache, from Purepecha kwarachi (“sandal”).
s: The huaraches he wore looked like dried and blackened fish lashed to the floors of his feet.

d: Someone who assumes leadership of a movement or activity
ety: From Middle English belwether, belleweder, equivalent to bell + wether (“castrated ram”).
s: Mortgage delinquencies often act as a bellwether for a forthcoming recession.

d: A vehicle carrying many passengers; used for public transport
ety: Borrowed from French char-à-bancs (literally “carriage with benches”).
s: Nevertheless, I felt responsible. I'd started the whole charabanc. It was my band.

d: Formal and explicit approval
ety: From Latin imprimātur (“let it be printed”), third person singular present subjunctive passive form of imprimere (“to imprint”).
s: Even with the imprimatur of Tynan and Hobson, the play was not an instant hit.

d: Euphemisms for death (based on an analogy between lying in a bed and in a tomb)
ety: Short for Medieval Latin quiētus est (literally “he is quiet”). First attested in the 1530s. Earlier attested as Late Middle English quietus est. Doublet of coy, quiet, quit, and quite.
s: The very unromantically accoutred form of a keen-visaged, middle-aged female, padding heavily in bedroom slippers along the garden walk, gave its quietus to the situation.

d: Someone who purchases and maintains an inventory of goods to be sold
ety: The noun is derived from Middle English mongere, mangere (“dealer, merchant, trader”), from Old English mangere (“dealer, merchant, trader”), from Proto-West Germanic *mangārī (“dealer, merchant, monger”), from Latin mangō (“dealer, trader”) + Proto-West Germanic *-ārī (suffix forming agent nouns, especially denoting occupations). The further etymology of mangō is uncertain; the following possibil
s: For the freshest wild catch, ask your monger when the fish are running.

d: A flared ruffle attached to the waistline of a dress or jacket or blouse
ety: From Latin peplum, from Ancient Greek πέπλον (péplon), accusative singular of πέπλος (péplos).
s: Over this they adopted the Greek peplum, under the name of palla. This garment, however, was exclusively confined to the gentler sex, and was never worn, as was the peplum among the Greeks, by men.

d: Music consisting of a single vocal part (usually with accompaniment)
ety: From Latin monodia, from Ancient Greek μονῳδία (monōidía).
s: All directions in life were blocked to him. He could not think, he could not sleep, his heart thudded to a deadening monody of fear. Fear that is itself the penalty of all things feared.

d: Disdainfully or ironically humorous; scornful and mocking
ety: From French sardonique, from Latin sardonius, from Ancient Greek σαρδόνιος (sardónios), alternative form of σαρδάνιος (sardánios, “bitter or scornful laughter”), which is often cited as deriving from the Sardinian plant (Ranunculus sardous or possibly Oenanthe crocata), known as either σαρδάνη (sardánē) or σαρδόνιον (sardónion). When eaten, it would cause the eater's face to contort in a look rese
s: He distances himself from people with his nasty, sardonic laughter.

d: A roll of ribbon
ety: Borrowed from French rouleau.
s: We always judge of others by ourselves; and his idea of Cupid's quiver is a rouleau.

d: Give expression to
ety: From Middle French évincer, from Latin ēvincō (“conquer entirely, prevail over; prove exhaustively”), from ē- (short form of ex- (intensive prefix)) + vincō (“conquer”). Doublet of evict.
s: Common sense and experience will and must evince the truth of this.

d: Lacking definite form or limits
ety: Inherited from Middle English nebulous, from Middle French nebuleus, from Latin nebulōsus (“full of mist, foggy, cloudy”), from nebula (“mist, vapour, cloud”), from Proto-Indo-European *nébʰos (“cloud, vapor, fog, moist, sky”). By surface analysis, nebula + -ous. More at neveling, nuel. Cognates * Ancient Greek νέφος (néphos, “cloud”) * German Nebel ** Old High German nebul (“cloud, fog”) * Old En
s: The mothers in NaturalMoms discussed nebulous fears about potential harms from vaccines and their distrust of the medical professionals who promoted a universal immunization schedule.

d: A situation in golf where an opponent’s ball blocks the line between your ball and the hole
ety: From the meaning in golf (where the stymie ball blocks the other ball from "seeing" the hole), perhaps from Scots stymie, stimie (“person with poor eyesight”), from Scots stime (“the least bit”). Or from Scots styme (“tiny bit, glimmer”) as in se nocht ane styme (“not to see a glimmer (of something)”). If so, it is a doublet of stime.
s: Mary, will you be mine? Shall we go round together? Will you fix up a match with me on the links of life which shall end only when the Grim Reaper lays us both a stymie?

d: The driver of a team of horses doing hauling
ety: From team + -ster.
s: He turned to the man who spoke. He wore long moustaches after the fashion of teamsters and he wore a widebrim hat with a low round crown.

d: A verse line having five metrical feet
ety: From Middle French pentamètre, by surface analysis, penta- + meter.
s: The best verses, more especially pentameters, are written on the principle of attracting and fixing the attention to their close.

d: Someone who buys large quantities of goods and resells to merchants rather than to the ultimate customers
ety: From job + -er.
s: It is usually best to choose a book jobber to handle the bulk of a library's purchases.

d: Brief and to the point; effectively cut short
ety: From Latin Lacōnicus (“Spartan”), from Ancient Greek Λακωνικός (Lakōnikós, “Laconian”). Laconia was the region inhabited and ruled by the Spartans, who were known for their brevity in speech.
s: His sense was strong and his style laconic.

d: An early form of sextant
ety: From Middle English astrelabie et al., from Middle French astrolabe, Old French astrelabe, from Ancient Greek ἀστρολάβος (astrolábos, “star-taking”), from ἄστρον (ástron, “star”) + λαμβάνω (lambánō, “I take”).
s: The shop carries more than a dozen sundials, mostly of bronze, plus an astrolabe ($650) of wrought iron.

d: Ill-mannered and coarse and contemptible in behavior or appearance
ety: From lout + -ish.
s: He was a loutish fellow, much bent in the shoulders, with leggings, which lacked most of the buttons, over his disreputable breeks.

d: Make believe with the intent to deceive
ety: First attested in the beginning of the 15th century, in Middle English; inherited from Middle English dissemblen, dissimblen, dissemelen, borrowed from Old French dessambler, dissembler, disembler, itself borrowed from Latin dissimulō and modified after sembler, semblance, etc. Doublet of dissimulate, dissimilate, and dissimule. Displaced native Old English mīþan.
s: Dissemble all your griefs and discontents.

d: A shrill grating or chirping noise made by some insects by rubbing body parts together
ety: 1838, from earlier term stridulous; from Latin strīdulus (“giving a shrill sound, creaking”), from strīdō (“utter a shrill or harsh sound; creak, shriek, grate, hiss”).
s: The Demons were crying now too, a stridulation that rose above the clamor and seemed to pierce the skull.
